name: Canary Releases and Prompt Flags
question: How do I ship a change without betting all traffic on it?
summary: Release a new prompt, model or tool version to a small slice of live traffic behind a feature flag, compare it with the control group on the same metrics, and widen in steps, such as 1%, 5%, 25% and 100%, only while guardrail metrics hold. A canary needs enough requests to tell a real drop from noise, so its size and duration come from statistics, not habit.
useCases: A prompt or model change that passed offline evals but still carries risk
Upgrading to a new model snapshot
High-volume traffic where a bad change would hurt many users quickly

items.detail: decides per request which variant runs, sticky per user
hash of a stable id, so a user stays in one group
1% → 5% → 25% → 100%, with a bake time at each step
success rate, judge score, latency, cost, escalations
is the canary’s success rate really lower than control’s?
flip the flag off when a guardrail is breached

steps: Pass offline evals first; a canary is the last gate, not the only one
Bucket users by a hash of a stable id and log the variant on every trace
Size the stage so a meaningful drop is detectable, then bake
Widen only while guardrails hold; roll back automatically when one breaks
pitfalls: A canary too small to detect a 4-point drop gives false comfort
Comparing canary and control from different hours or user groups
Per-request randomisation that flips a user between variants mid-conversation
remember: Small slice, enough samples, widen only while guardrails hold.

steps.title: Define the ladder
steps.text: The new prompt goes to 1%, then 5%, 25% and finally everyone. Each stage is a checkpoint where it can still be stopped.

steps.title: Bucket users, not requests
steps.text: A hash of the user id gives a number between 0 and 1. Below the share, the user gets v13, and keeps getting it on every request.

steps.title: Tag every trace with the variant
steps.text: Online evals, dashboards and alerts can then split every metric by canary and control.

steps.title: Bake until the evidence is enough
steps.text: With fewer than about 350 canary requests, a 4-point drop is hard to tell from noise, so the stage waits.

steps.title: Test, and roll back automatically
steps.text: A one-sided two-proportion test asks whether the canary is worse. At 5%: 600 requests at 90.2% against 94.1% for control, p < 0.001, so the flag goes to 0%.

steps.title: Promote stage by stage
steps.text: If the canary holds, the share moves to the next rung. Each rung repeats the bake and the test.

pros: Limits the blast radius of a bad change
Measures real users, not just test sets
The same flags allow instant kill switches
cons: Needs enough traffic for a statistically clear answer
Flag and variant plumbing through every layer
Conversation-level metrics are noisier than per-request ones
avoidWhen: Very low traffic, where a canary cannot reach a meaningful sample in reasonable time
Changes that must reach everyone at once, such as a regulatory fix

practice.scenario: A food-delivery platform wants a new refund-policy prompt for its support agent. It passed the offline suite, but refunds are money. The new version goes to 5% of users behind a flag, bucketed by a hash of the user id. After 12 hours the canary’s resolution rate is 90.2% against 94.1% for control on 1,200 canary conversations, so the flag is turned off automatically.

practice.analogy: A new dish on a small table first. If those diners send it back, the kitchen never serves it to the whole restaurant.

library.name: OpenFeature
library.what: A vendor-neutral feature-flag API; plug in a provider such as LaunchDarkly, Unleash or flagd and evaluate flags per user.

practice.note: Log the variant on every trace, so dashboards and online evals can be split by canary and control.

samples.code:
from openfeature import api
from openfeature.evaluation_context import EvaluationContext
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest

flags = api.get_client()          # configure a provider (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, flagd...) at startup

def pick_prompt(user_id: str) -> str:
    ctx = EvaluationContext(targeting_key=user_id)          # sticky per user
    return flags.get_string_value("refund-prompt-version", "v12", ctx)

def canary_is_worse(ok_canary, n_canary, ok_control, n_control, max_drop=0.02):
    """One-sided test: is the canary's success rate lower than control's?"""
    z, p = proportions_ztest([ok_canary, ok_control], [n_canary, n_control],
                             alternative="smaller")
    drop = ok_control / n_control - ok_canary / n_canary
    return p < 0.05 and drop > max_drop

# 1,200 canary conversations at 90.2% vs 22,800 control at 94.1%
print(canary_is_worse(1082, 1200, 21455, 22800))   # True: roll back

numericDrill.question: Your service handles 2,000 requests an hour. The canary gets 5% of traffic for 6 hours. If the new prompt is truly 4 points worse, how many extra failed requests will the canary have caused by the end?
numericDrill.answer: Canary requests: 2,000 × 0.05 × 6 = 600. Extra failures: 600 × 0.04 = 24. The same change at 100% for 6 hours would have caused 2,000 × 6 × 0.04 = 480.

interview.question: How do you decide how long a canary must run?
interview.answer: From the smallest drop you care about and your traffic. For a drop from 94% to 90%, a one-sided test with 80% power needs roughly 450 canary requests; at 5% of 2,000 requests an hour that is about 4.5 hours. Also bake long enough to cover the daily traffic mix.

interview.question: Why bucket by user rather than by request?
interview.answer: So each user sees one variant consistently. Flipping variants mid-conversation confuses users and contaminates metrics, because a failure could come from either version. A hash of a stable id gives sticky, random assignment.

mistakes.mistake: Declaring the canary safe after 50 requests
mistakes.fix: Size each stage so the drop you care about is detectable

mistakes.mistake: Comparing the canary with last week’s numbers
mistakes.fix: Compare with a concurrent control group on the same metrics

quiz.question: A new refund prompt passed offline evals. How should it reach users?
options: To everyone at once, since evals passed
To a small share behind a flag, compared with control, then widened in steps
Only to staff, forever
Randomly to half of all requests with no comparison
quiz.explanation: A canary is the last gate: a small slice, a concurrent control and gradual widening.

quiz.question: A telecom’s plan-recommendation agent gets 2,000 conversations an hour. A canary runs at 5% for 6 hours. How many canary conversations is that?
In that 600-conversation canary, the new prompt is truly 3 points worse. How many extra failed conversations did the canary cause?
quiz.explanation: 600 × 0.03 = 18, against 360 if the whole service had run it for the same 6 hours.

quiz.question: Why should canary assignment hash a stable user id rather than draw a random number per request?
options: It is faster to compute
It hides the variant from logs
So each user sees one version consistently and metrics can be attributed
Random numbers are not allowed in Python
quiz.explanation: Per-request draws mix versions within a conversation and blur the comparison.

quiz.question: A canary’s success rate is compared with the control group. Which practices make the comparison valid? Select all that apply.
options: Control and canary run over the same period
The variant is recorded on every trace
Compare the canary with last month’s average
Put all premium users in the canary
quiz.explanation: A concurrent control and variant tags make groups comparable; old baselines and biased assignment do not.

quiz.question: A canary of 40 conversations shows 90% success against 94% for control. What should you conclude?
options: The new version is worse; roll back
The new version is fine
The sample is too small to tell a 4-point difference from noise
Increase the share to 100%
quiz.explanation: With 40 conversations the standard error is about 4.7 points, as large as the difference itself.

quiz.question: Roughly how many canary conversations are needed to detect a drop from 94% to 90% with about 80% power in a one-sided test?
options: About 35
About 350
About 3,500
About 35,000
quiz.explanation: n ≈ ((1.645 + 0.84) × 0.3 / 0.04)² ≈ 350 when the control group is large.

quiz.question: Why does proving a 1-point improvement take far more traffic than catching a 4-point drop?
options: Improvements are measured differently
Flags are slower for improvements
The required sample grows with the inverse square of the difference, so a quarter of the effect needs about sixteen times the data
It does not; both need the same sample
quiz.explanation: Halving the effect quadruples the sample; a 1-point gain needs about sixteen times more than a 4-point drop.

quiz.question: Which metrics make sensible guardrails for a rebooking-prompt canary? Select all that apply.
options: Task success rate
p95 latency
Number of lines in the prompt
The engineer’s confidence
quiz.explanation: Guardrails are live outcome metrics such as success, latency, cost and escalations.

quiz.question: A broker’s canary guardrail is breached at 2 a.m. What should happen?
options: Wait for the morning stand-up
Widen the canary to get more data
Page someone to edit the prompt live
The flag turns the canary off automatically and alerts the owner
quiz.explanation: Automatic rollback limits harm; the investigation can happen after.

quiz.question: Which is the typical order of canary stages?
quiz.explanation: Start small and widen in steps, baking and checking at each one.

quiz.question: A health app has only 300 conversations a day. Which statements about canarying there are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A canary may never reach a meaningful sample in reasonable time
Stronger offline evals and careful review matter more
A 1% canary for one hour is enough
Canary statistics work the same at any traffic level
quiz.explanation: Low traffic makes live comparisons slow and noisy, so offline evidence must carry more weight.

quiz.question: Which tool provides a vendor-neutral feature-flag API with pluggable providers?
options: OpenFeature
Temporal
Evidently
pybreaker
quiz.explanation: OpenFeature standardises flag evaluation; LaunchDarkly, Unleash and others plug in as providers.

quiz.question: Argo Rollouts canaries a new agent image by shifting pods. What can it not do on its own that a prompt flag can?
options: Roll back automatically
Keep each user on one variant across requests
Shift traffic gradually
Read Prometheus metrics
quiz.explanation: Pod-level canaries route requests, not users; per-user stickiness needs a flag or routing on a user key.

quiz.question: A KYC-extraction prompt canary shows a higher manual-review rate but the same accuracy. Which actions are sensible? Select all that apply.
options: Treat manual-review rate as a guardrail and roll back if it breaches
Investigate which documents trigger extra reviews
Ignore it because accuracy is unchanged
Widen immediately to collect more data
quiz.explanation: Guardrails exist for costs like manual review; investigate before widening.

quiz.question: At 5% for 12 hours, a canary shows 90.2% against 94.1% for control, p < 0.001. What is the right decision?
options: Roll back
Promote to 25%
Extend the bake to a week
Ignore the result
quiz.explanation: The drop is large and statistically clear, so the guardrail says roll back.

quiz.question: The canary’s success equals control’s after a well-sized stage. What is the right next step?
options: Roll back to be safe
Promote to the next stage and bake again
Stop the experiment and keep 5% forever
Switch the control group to the canary
quiz.explanation: No detectable harm at the right sample size is the signal to widen.

quiz.question: A bank’s prompt canary covers weekday mornings only. Why can that give a false picture? Select all that apply.
options: Traffic mix differs on evenings and weekends
Some problems appear only for request types that are rare in the morning
Morning users are always more accurate
Canaries must never run in the morning
quiz.explanation: Bake long enough to cover the daily and weekly traffic mix.

quiz.question: A canary is run for a new model snapshot rather than a prompt. What should the flag control?
options: The trace backend
The snapshot name in the release used for that user
The user’s mobile plan
The span names
quiz.explanation: The flag selects which release, including the snapshot, serves each user.

quiz.question: Which of these can a canary catch that offline evals may miss? Select all that apply.
options: Behaviour on real inputs that the test set never covered
Latency and cost under real load
Syntax errors in the prompt template file
A model alias moved by the provider last month
quiz.explanation: Live traffic reveals real inputs and load; template syntax fails earlier, and provider moves are not your release.
